A.description: Dispositions and Responsibility: This strand focuses on what data is and all of the ways students should think about and frame it as a concept and tool. The nature of data is complex, diverse, and humanistic. When engaging with data you must consider the form it takes, where it can come from, and what it can and should be used for. Working with data is non-linear and often raises new questions while seeking answers to others. Additionally the data process is influenced at all stages by the humans working with it which can lead to biases and concerns about ethics and responsibility. However, data can also be powerful for supporting the advancement of discovery or enactment of change.

A1.description: Nature of Data: The nature of data is complex, variably, humanistic, and often incomplete. Data can take many forms and may come from many different sources. Additionally, data is integral to the field of AI.

A.1.1.description: Data types and forms: Recognize that data can exist as quantitative, ordinal, categorical, and other values. Data also can be “nontraditional” forms such as graphical or other media.

3-5.A.1.1a.description: Distinguish when data is categorical versus numeric and define the difference.

6-8.A.1.1a.description: Analyze the way categorical and numeric data shapes its interpretation and analysis.

9-10.A.1.1a.description: Define "qualitative" and "quantitative" and understand how they relate to categorical and numeric data.

11-12.A.1.1a.description: Recognize that multiple types of data can provide valuable insights into the same inquiry.

3-5.A.1.1b.description: Recognize that non-traditional forms (e.g., photographs, written text, audio recordings) of data are informative and supportive of inquiry.

6-8.A.1.1b.description: Recognize that numerical variables may be either discrete or continuous.

9-10.A.1.1b.description: Understand that forms of media (e.g., photographs, written text, audio recordings) can be represented in quantitative and qualitative terms.

3-5.A.1.1c.description: Understand case structure as a way to identify the defining "case" of the data where a case is a data point which may have many variables associated with it, each with a possible value.

A.1.2.description: Data are produced by people: Recognize that data represent decisions about measurement and inclusion involving people who are and are not immediately present.

3-5.A.1.2a.description: Ask questions about how data are collected or considered.

6-8.A.1.2a.description: Ask questions regarding the origins of specific automated measures (e.g., webtracking, email meta-data, user accounts).

9-10.A.1.2a.description: Explain how data-based decisions are revisited as new evidence or societal needs emerge (e.g., blood pressure cut-off numbers, dietary guidance, medical benchmarks).

11-12.A.1.2a.description: Explore the origins of some standardized unit measurements (e.g., horsepower, mole, scores on AP exams).

3-5.A.1.2b.description: Understand that data is generated by people who make decisions about what and how to measure.

6-8.A.1.2b.description: Recognize the limits of the information the data can provide and the story it can tell.

9-10.A.1.2b.description: Evaluate why data models require updates to maintain accuracy and relevance.

11-12.A.1.2b.description: Identify the risks and tradeoffs of using traditional measurements (e.g., IQ, BMI).

6-8.A.1.2c.description: Recognize that conclusions may need to be revised in the future as more knowledge and data become available.

A.1.3.description: Variability of data: Recognize that variability is a foundational component of data.

3-5.A.1.3a.description: Multiple conclusions can be drawn from the same set of data.

6-8.A.1.3a.description: Make sense of the variability of data through an iterative process of refinement by questioning.

9-10.A.1.3a.description: Recognize the different types of variability (e.g., natural, measurement, sampling).

11-12.A.1.3a.description: Explore different types of variability for making inferences (e.g., confidence intervals, various tests, classification models).

3-5.A.1.3b.description: Recognize that variability of data contributes to uncertainty. e.g., measuring plant growth daily shows natural variation which makes predicting exact height for the next day difficult

A.1.4.description: Data provides partial information: Recognize that data captures certain aspects of a model of a target phenomenon or set of objects in the world but does not represent it completely.

3-5.A.1.4a.description: Select variables of interest for data investigations while recognizing those selections will retain inherent limits.

6-8.A.1.4a.description: Specify ways that data provide incomplete information relative to the object being studied.

9-10.A.1.4a.description: Evaluate claims derived from data by questioning how phenomena are measured, categorized, or represented.

11-12.A.1.4a.description: Design and compare alternative data representations, justifying choices to address inherent uncertainty.

6-8.A.1.4b.description: Approach data and evidence-based claims with reasonable skepticism and apply the process of evaluating the validity of claims while remaining open-minded.

A.1.5.description: Data and AI: Recognize that data “fuels” AI, that AI can be compared to a function machine (math), algorithm (CS), or a prediction model (statistics) that relies on data to both operate and improve itself, and that AI tools can also be used to analyze complex data in research.

3-5.A.1.5a.description: Recognize AI as a computing tool that adapts its functions by acquiring knowledge from organized data inputs and outputs. e.g., AI tools improve their tasks by comparing outputs to correct answers such as a photo-sorting app checks if its ‘cat’ labels match human-provided tags, then updates its sorting rules to reduce mistakes

6-8.A.1.5a.description: Describe in plain language how AI uses and builds upon data in multiple ways. e.g., AI systems identify patterns in data by processing thousands of input-output pairs, and the system adjusts its internal mathematical model to minimize error, enabling it to predict outputs for new inputs such as a spam filter

9-10.A.1.5a.description: Describe the basic mathematical features of an AI model in terms of independent variables (e.g., inputs), dependent variables (e.g., outputs), and predictors or weights (e.g., slopes of many variables). e.g., AI models use math to weigh inputs, such as a music recommendation model might calculate: (play_count × weight₁) + (listen_duration × weight₂) + (skip_count × weight₃) = recommendation_score, and weights are adjusted automatically to minimize mismatches between predicted and actual user preferences.

11-12.A.1.5a.description: Identify and label a simple prediction algorithm or equation for a very basic AI prediction model. e.g., a basic AI model’s equation looks like: Prediction = (weight₁ × input₁) + (weight₂ × input₂), such as a college admission model might weight GPA (input₁) and test scores (input₂) to output an acceptance likelihood, and training involves automatically adjusting weights to match historical data.

3-5.A.1.5b.description: Recognize that many inputs and outputs can be organized into a structure that is easily readable by a machine (e.g., data-table).

6-8.A.1.5b.description: Identify how issues in data, such as bias, missing data, and errors, can affect the output of an AI tool and the training of an AI tool from the input-output pairs it learns from. e.g., If AI only sees pictures of cats in sunlight, it would fail to recognize cats in shadows

9-10.A.1.5b.description: Describe and explore how it is possible for data in a variety of formats (e.g., images) to be translated into organized, numerical information for an AI model to process.

11-12.A.1.5b.description: Understand that algorithms use cost functions to measure errors and adjust predictions.

9-10.A.1.5c.description: Identify how biases in training data can lead to biases in AI models by directly affecting predictors or weights. e.g., If AI only sees pictures of cats in sunlight, it would fail to recognize cats in shadows

11-12.A.1.5c.description: Recognize that some AI tools can be used to explore complex data with many variables.

11-12.A.1.5d.description: Recognize the types of problems that are ideal for using an AI tool to analyze complex data.

A2.description: Data Ethics and Responsibilities: The data process is influenced at all stages by the humans working with it which can lead to concerns about ethics and responsibility. It is important when working with data to consider the use risks as well as the benefits. Data can be powerful for supporting the advancement of discovery or enactment of change.

A.2.1.description: Data use risks and benefits: Recognize that data can pose risks but also benefits for individuals and groups, and understand its potential uses, limitations, and risks, including unintended consequences.

3-5.A.2.1a.description: Identify how data collection can create risks (e.g., medical information, location, privacy, exclusion) for individuals or groups, and describe ways to protect personal information.

6-8.A.2.1a.description: Describe how social groups can be inadequately represented by existing data and data schemes. e.g., city planners using traffic data collected from weekday commuters overlook nighttime workers' needs, such as poor bus schedules for nurses on night shifts

9-10.A.2.1a.description: Analyze how data use can perpetuate biases or systemic inequities (e.g., predictive policing, hiring algorithms).

11-12.A.2.1a.description: Recognize that data risk can change based on time, circumstance, and purpose.

3-5.A.2.1b.description: Evaluate how datasets can benefit society (e.g., solving problems, improving designs) while considering potential risks to individuals.

6-8.A.2.1b.description: Acknowledge that options and choices are available for data collected about individuals, and recognize that what is gathered or excluded can have consequences. e.g., a survey claiming "most teens love math" is biased if only the math club members completed the survey

9-10.A.2.1b.description: Evaluate context-specific risks and benefits of data interpretations (e.g., health tracking for improving care vs. privacy concerns).

11-12.A.2.1b.description: Identify data benefits that can appear well into the future and in unexpected ways.

A.2.2.description: Biases in data: Recognize all data contains bias but data collection and analysis methods can increase or mitigate the effects of biases.

3-5.A.2.2a.description: Recognize that some biases in data are neutral, while others can be harmful when making decisions and inferences, and some may not cause harm at all. e.g., neutral, preference of apples over oranges in a fruit study; harmful, surveying the coding club to generalize about all students

6-8.A.2.2a.description: Identify how biases in data affect inferences and questions.

9-10.A.2.2a.description: Recognize how biases can obscure inferences drawn from data.

11-12.A.2.2a.description: Propose multiple perspectives on data to mitigate inherent biases.

3-5.A.2.2b.description: Understand the importance of considering the context, scope, and purpose of data in order to mitigate bias.

9-10.A.2.2b.description: Consider how the consolidation or combination of different data can create additional biases.

11-12.A.2.2b.description: Understand the difference between implicit and explicit bias.

A.2.3.description: Power of data: Recognize data empowers discovery, decision-making, and advocacy across fields.

3-5.A.2.3a.description: Compare arguments with and without data.

6-8.A.2.3a.description: Analyze how data is used to solve problems, persuade, and discover new ideas.

9-10.A.2.3a.description: Evaluate how data drives innovation in fields and informs community choices.

11-12.A.2.3a.description: Use data to support arguments, design solutions, or challenge inequities.

11-12.A.2.3b.description: Investigate case studies where data advanced scientific, economic, or social progress.

11-12.A.2.3c.description: Identify when data alone is insufficient and complementary methods are needed. e.g., Data may quantify the number of people affected by a policy, but personal testimonies are needed to illustrate its human impact

A3.description: Investigative Dispositions: Working with data is non-linear and often requires cycling between phases in various orders multiple times. The process of investigating with data often raises new questions while seeking answers to others. Additionally, data is influenced by the humans working with it and the contexts within which they work.

A.3.1.description: The investigative process: Recognize that making sense with data requires engaging with it in a particular way that includes combinations of the concepts and practices in the other four strands.

3-5.A.3.1a.description: Plan and conduct investigations to answer questions using basic data organization and visualization.

6-8.A.3.1a.description: Investigate real-world questions by cleaning, analyzing, and interpreting data to draw conclusions.

9-10.A.3.1a.description: Design and refine investigations to address contextual problems (e.g., social, educational, business, medical, governmental issues), evaluating limitations and biases.

11-12.A.3.1a.description: Conduct independent investigations to inform decisions, leveraging advanced tools and addressing uncertainty.

11-12.A.3.1b.description: Compare investigative approaches across fields to critique strengths and limitations.

A.3.2.description: Iteration: Recognize that the investigative process is not linear but cyclic and iterative, with many of the phases repeating and looping back.

3-5.A.3.2a.description: Revise questions and methods at each stage of investigation based on new findings.

6-8.A.3.2a.description: Recognize that the investigative process is non-linear, often cycling between phases in various orders multiple times.

9-10.A.3.2a.description: Employ iteration in an investigation to strengthen interpretations or inspire new investigations.

11-12.A.3.2a.description: Propose new approaches for leveraging the investigative process to strengthen inferences and arguments.

A.3.3.description: Dynamic inferences: Recognize that inferences from data are dynamic, evolving with new data and additional analysis.

3-5.A.3.3a.description: Explain how inferences shift as new data emerges during an investigation.

6-8.A.3.3a.description: Revise initial conclusions when new data emerges and use evidence to support claims.

9-10.A.3.3a.description: Use digital tools to test and refine inferences from large or complex datasets.

11-12.A.3.3a.description: Critically evaluate and update inferences as data scales or methods advance.

A.3.4.description: Apply context: Recognize that the context surrounding the data and the investigation shapes interpretation. Many fields (biology vs. psychology; economics vs. sociology) have created very different frameworks to organize problems. Considering multiple approaches may reveal useful insights from the same data.

3-5.A.3.4a.description: Recognize that data interpretation varies across social and cultural contexts.

6-8.A.3.4a.description: Explain data interpretations from various disciplinary and community perspectives (e.g., social studies, families).

9-10.A.3.4a.description: Reinterpret data from multiple perspectives, disciplines, and historical frames of reference.

11-12.A.3.4a.description: Interpret data drawn from different fields and topics based on accepted norms within those fields.

9-10.A.3.4b.description: Compare and contrast problem solving approaches and the resulting findings.

11-12.A.3.4b.description: Compare multiple problem-solving approaches, and identify how those differences may compound over time and when repeated.

A.3.5.description: Student data agency: Cultivate the motivation to engage with data in all areas of life and understand how data impacts your own experiences.

3-5.A.3.5a.description: Describe the ways in which data can affect your personal life and habits.

6-8.A.3.5a.description: Embed data practices into everyday life and advocate for the benefits of doing so.

9-10.A.3.5a.description: Utilize data science tools and methods to engage in personal and collective inquiry relevant to one’s own life and interests.

11-12.A.3.5a.description: Establish accountability by basing claims and decisions on relevant data.

6-8.A.3.5b.description: Assess the accuracy, perspective, credibility, and relevance of various resources (e.g., information, media, data).

11-12.A.3.5b.description: Explore career fields and their intersection with data collection, curation, storytelling, and societal impact.

B.description: Creation and Curation: This strand focuses on where data comes from and how it should be collected, organized, and formatted in order to make it useful. Data collected from real world scenarios is often complex and messy, and whether it is collected first hand, or retrieved second hand from an external source, it requires curation and cleaning before analysis. The context of data collection matters and affects the nature of errors in data collection. The methods and decisions made during data collection affect the usefulness of the data and its ability to answer different questions.

B1.description: Organization and Processing: In order for data to be useful for analysis and visualization, it often needs to be organized and formatted in particular ways. Organization can include both procedural cleaning up of errors or mistakes and processing or transforming the data through calculations and logic statements to create new or summative measures.

B.1.1.description: Data cleaning: Identify and address data quality issues to ensure accuracy and reliability, progressing from simple error identification to using systematic approaches.

3-5.B.1.1a.description: Look through data to identify missing data, and add additional cases or values for variables if needed.

6-8.B.1.1a.description: Informally identify anomalies and outliers in a distribution of data and make an informed decision as to whether those observations should be removed or filtered out for analysis.

9-10.B.1.1a.description: Use data dictionaries to identify codes for missing or incomplete data (e.g., NA, 99999, 0, " "), and either recode or filter data to remove those observations.

11-12.B.1.1a.description: Develop comprehensive data validation procedures, including automated checks.

3-5.B.1.1b.description: Look through data to identify unreasonable values or recording errors in data values, and correct these if the correct values are known.

9-10.B.1.1b.description: Apply basic cross-validation techniques to verify data quality across multiple sources, including source comparison, split sampling, internal consistency checks, and domain range validation.

11-12.B.1.1b.description: Implement verification protocols for complex datasets with multiple dependencies.

B.1.2.description: Organizing and structure: Organize raw data into structured formats using categories, tables, and systematic recording methods.

3-5.B.1.2a.description: Collect and organize data about objects or events with multiple variables, progressing from simple case cards to structured tables with labeled rows (e.g., observations) and columns (e.g., variables).

6-8.B.1.2a.description: Use categorical variables or bins/groups of numerical variables in a dataset to restructure data into groups.

9-10.B.1.2a.description: Create and manage complex data structures with multiple related tables, understanding primary and foreign key relationships between datasets.

11-12.B.1.2a.description: Develop and implement data organization systems that accommodate both structured and unstructured data types.

6-8.B.1.2b.description: Make sense of and use a dataset arranged in nested or hierarchical format.

9-10.B.1.2b.description: Transform and restructure hierarchical or nested data into normalized tabular formats suitable for analysis.

11-12.B.1.2b.description: Create scalable data organization strategies that maintain data integrity while handling missing values, irregular structures, and evolving data requirements.

9-10.B.1.2c.description: Design efficient organizational schemas for large datasets with multiple variables and complex relationships.

11-12.B.1.2c.description: Design and implement metadata documentation systems to track data lineage, transformations, and organizational structures.

B.1.3.description: Processing and transformation: Transform and manipulate data through sorting, grouping, filtering, and combining datasets.

3-5.B.1.3a.description: Manipulate tabular data by grouping cases based on categorical variables (e.g., grouping roller coaster cases so that all wood coasters are together and all steel coasters are together) and ordering cases based on numerical variables (e.g., ordering roller coaster cases "top speed" from slowest to fastest).

6-8.B.1.3a.description: Use existing numerical variables to create bins or groups based on benchmark values appropriate for the context, or bins based on numerical ranges (e.g., 0-4, 5-10, 11-15, etc...).

9-10.B.1.3a.description: Use calculations and logic statements to create new categorical variables based on existing categorical (e.g., if(employment=”employed”, Yes, No)) or quantitative variables (e.g., if(weight<30, light, if(weight>60,heavy ,medium)).

11-12.B.1.3a.description: Use an identifying variable (e.g., index, case ID) to merge two separate datasets that have the same observation, but contain different variables to merge datasets together.

6-8.B.1.3b.description: Create a new variable from an existing variable that transforms (e.g., uses a formula to convert units of measure) or recodes data (e.g., blue-->B, red--> R).

9-10.B.1.3b.description: Filter data based on groups or subsets of data relevant to the problem and context.

11-12.B.1.3b.description: Use appropriate procedures to join two datasets together that have different observations with the same variables measured.

B.1.4.description: Summarizing groups: Calculate and analyze group-level statistics from detailed data to reveal patterns and relationships.

3-5.B.1.4a.description: Compare characteristics across groups using basic numerical summaries (e.g., comparing the typical recess activity across different grade levels).

6-8.B.1.4a.description: Use summary measures of groups within a nested or hierarchical dataset.

9-10.B.1.4a.description: Create summary measures for groups that can then be used as a measure at the group level (e.g., for salary data, compute average salary for different occupational groups).

11-12.B.1.4a.description: Use datasets with derived variables, based on other variables in the dataset.

3-5.B.1.4b.description: Create basic summaries that describe what is the same or different about groups in a dataset (e.g., summarizing how children of different ages differ in their favorite sports).

B2.description: Designing for Data Collection: The design of a data investigation is as important as the data collection process. Framing a data-based investigation requires identifying a problem or question to be explored. Additionally, the methods must be carefully chosen and the values and tradeoffs considered.

B.2.1.description: Designing data-based investigations: Identify problems and formulate questions that guide meaningful data collection and analysis.

3-5.B.2.1a.description: Design an investigation requiring collection of data involving the collection or gathering of multiple variables.

6-8.B.2.1a.description: Construct data-based questions that explore relationships between variables and consider how data collection methods affect the quality of evidence.

9-10.B.2.1a.description: Construct data-based questions about the design of a study to determine causality and make predictions.

11-12.B.2.1a.description: Construct data-based questions that address complex systems with multiple interacting variables, including consideration of confounding factors and effect modifiers.

3-5.B.2.1b.description: Design an investigation that require collecting numerical data, including looking at a variable over a period of time.

9-10.B.2.1b.description: Identify comparison and association data-based questions appropriate for addressing problems of interest.

11-12.B.2.1b.description: Design research questions that incorporate multiple levels of analysis and account for both direct and indirect relationships between variables.

11-12.B.2.1c.description: Formulate questions that address the validity and reliability of data collection methods, including considerations of systematic bias and measurement error.

B.2.2.description: Data creation techniques and methods: Explore various ways to generate data through simulations, sensors, and automated collection methods.

3-5.B.2.2a.description: Record outcomes of simple random simulations or processes.

6-8.B.2.2a.description: Use data generated from simulations and models to investigate a question of interest.

9-10.B.2.2a.description: Describe benefits and drawbacks of using proxy variables.

11-12.B.2.2a.description: Design simulations (e.g., using an RNG or computer software) and underlying models to generate data specific to a problem of interest.

3-5.B.2.2b.description: Use data generated by sensors or automated techniques. e.g., weather stations record temperature every hour

6-8.B.2.2b.description: Deploy or trigger sensors or automated data collection methods and use the generated data to investigate a pre-defined problem or question.

9-10.B.2.2b.description: Use and/or change parameters of simulations to generate data to address a problem of interest.

11-12.B.2.2b.description: Identify optimal sensors or automated data collection methods for answering a data-based question or designing an experiment.

3-5.B.2.2c.description: Describe the procedures and tools to be used to measure a quantity of an object or an event.

9-10.B.2.2c.description: Design sensor-based experiments or automated data collection scenarios to explore a problem or question and identify the scenarios' limitations and trade-offs.

11-12.B.2.2c.description: Distinguish between surveys, observational studies, and experiments.

9-10.B.2.2d.description: Describe the features, benefits, limitations, and ethical thinking that went into a data collection process.

9-10.B.2.2e.description: Design and implement traditional data collection methods (e.g., surveys, observations, field studies) to investigate research questions and evaluate their strengths and limitations compared to automated approaches.

B.2.3.description: Creating data collection plans: Develop systematic plans that specify what data to collect, how to collect it, and from what sources to answer investigation questions.

3-5.B.2.3a.description: Create a basic data collection plan that specifies what data to gather, what tools to use, and what sources to access for an investigation.

6-8.B.2.3a.description: Design data collection plans that include data types needed, collection methods, sample sizes, and timing considerations for investigations.

9-10.B.2.3a.description: Develop comprehensive data collection plans that address potential limitations, specify quality control measures, and include contingency strategies.

11-12.B.2.3a.description: Create sophisticated data collection plans that incorporate ethical considerations, cost-benefit analysis, and protocols for ensuring data integrity and reproducibility.

B.2.4.description: Finding secondary data: Explore, locate, evaluate, and retrieve datasets collected by others to address research questions and data investigations.

3-5.B.2.4a.description: Locate and retrieve simple datasets from educational resources and child-friendly data repositories to investigate specific questions.

6-8.B.2.4a.description: Search for and retrieve appropriate datasets from educational repositories and curated sources designed for middle school investigations.

9-10.B.2.4a.description: Locate and retrieve relevant datasets from publicly available scientific, civic, or government databases using search tools and filters.

11-12.B.2.4a.description: Identify (and know you can request access to) non-publicly available datasets by contacting researchers, reading scientific literature, or communicating with public officials.

3-5.B.2.4b.description: Identify basic criteria for determining whether a dataset is relevant to a given question (e.g., topic match, timeframe, geographic relevance).

6-8.B.2.4b.description: Evaluate potential datasets based on relevance, timeliness, and credibility of the source for answering specific questions.

9-10.B.2.4b.description: Evaluate datasets from multiple sources to determine which best addresses a research question, considering factors such as data quality, sample size, and collection methods.

11-12.B.2.4b.description: Develop strategies for finding and accessing datasets that require special permissions, logins, or formal data requests.

6-8.B.2.4c.description: Use metadata and documentation to understand the context and limitations of secondary datasets.

9-10.B.2.4c.description: Use data catalogs, repositories, and open data portals to find datasets that meet specific criteria for investigations.

11-12.B.2.4c.description: Evaluate and navigate licensing and citation requirements when using secondary data sources for research.

11-12.B.2.4d.description: Combine multiple secondary datasets to create more comprehensive or useful data for specific investigations.

B3.description: Measurement and Datafication: The methods and decisions made during data collection affect the usefulness of the data and its ability to answer different questions. It is important to consider the potential effects of methodological decisions when collecting data and to determine the methodological decisions made by others when using secondary data. It is also important to consider ethical practices of using other's data.

B.3.1.description: Creating your own data: Collect, measure, and document data accurately using appropriate tools and methods.

3-5.B.3.1a.description: Understand that a variable measures the same characteristic on several individuals or objects.

6-8.B.3.1a.description: Create an ordinal scale of measurement.

9-10.B.3.1a.description: Create a data dictionary to document the data collection process.

11-12.B.3.1a.description: Evaluate and critique measurement validity, reliability, and bias in data collection methods, and design comprehensive datafication strategies that address ethical considerations and potential sources of measurement error.

3-5.B.3.1b.description: Recognize and apply measurement precision, including why repeated measurements may vary and how to choose appropriate precision levels.

6-8.B.3.1b.description: Understand that data is information collected and recorded with a purpose.

3-5.B.3.1c.description: Identify the characteristics of an event or object that can be measured.

6-8.B.3.1c.description: Distinguish between human-derived data from images, sounds, and text vs. computer-derived data from images, sounds, and text.

3-5.B.3.1d.description: Plan and conduct measurements by identifying measurable characteristics and collecting both categorical and numerical variables of objects/events.

B.3.2.description: Working with data created by others: Evaluate and interpret others' datasets by examining collection methods, context, and quality.

3-5.B.3.2a.description: Consider the reasonable values for each of the variables and note those that are suspect.

6-8.B.3.2a.description: Consider how the data were measured, with what tool and precision.

9-10.B.3.2a.description: Make use of metadata and data dictionary to understand a data set.

11-12.B.3.2a.description: Work with data collected over time and consider how to aggregate appropriately.

6-8.B.3.2b.description: Consider who collected these data and for what purpose.

9-10.B.3.2b.description: Consider who or what was included in the data collection and who or what was not.

11-12.B.3.2b.description: Work with data collected over space and consider how to aggregate appropriately.

6-8.B.3.2c.description: Consider when and where the data were collected.

11-12.B.3.2c.description: Create strategies for dealing with data that is constantly updated.

B.3.3.description: Ethics of data collection and usage: Collect and use data ethically, considering privacy, fairness, and potential impacts.

3-5.B.3.3a.description: Recognize that personal information needs to be used respectfully and that this hasn’t always been done in the past.

6-8.B.3.3a.description: Design data collection methods that address privacy, consent, and fair representation of different groups.

9-10.B.3.3a.description: Evaluate and address ethical implications of data collection choices, including privacy, bias, and representation.

11-12.B.3.3a.description: Develop data collection protocols that prevent bias, protect privacy, and ensure ethical representation across diverse populations.

3-5.B.3.3b.description: Consider how data categories might affect different people in different ways. e.g., asking students about the language they speak at home and not including that language as an option may make students feel excluded

6-8.B.3.3b.description: Examine historical examples of harmful data practices to inform ethical data use.

9-10.B.3.3b.description: Analyze existing datasets for potential bias, discrimination, or unfair representation.

11-12.B.3.3b.description: Apply validation techniques to prevent bias and ensure ethical use of secondary data, including AI tools.

B4.description: Complexity of Data: Data collected from real world scenarios is often complex across many dimensions including messiness, size, and structure. In order to be able to work with authentic real-world datasets of high complexity, these dimensions must be scaffolded such that increasingly higher levels of complexity are encountered as one approaches mastery.

B.4.1.description: Cleanliness: Work with datasets at increasing levels of cleanliness and identify how datasets need to be curated to address messiness issues.

3-5.B.4.1a.description: Work with datasets that require some cleaning (e.g., resolution of missing data or blank cells).

6-8.B.4.1a.description: Identify and handle missing values marked by special codes (-99) or blank cells.

9-10.B.4.1a.description: Work with datasets requiring multiple types of cleaning such as missing values, errors, and anomalies.

11-12.B.4.1a.description: Apply advanced data cleaning techniques to handle complex data quality issues such as outliers, inconsistencies, and systematic errors.

3-5.B.4.1b.description: Verify data by comparing recorded values to original sources when possible.

6-8.B.4.1b.description: Distinguish between true zero values and blank cells.

9-10.B.4.1b.description: Clean and prepare datasets before merging multiple sources.

11-12.B.4.1b.description: Develop and document reproducible data cleaning workflows that maintain data integrity.

11-12.B.4.1c.description: Evaluate and validate cleaned datasets using statistical methods and domain knowledge.

B.4.2.description: Complexity of variables: Explore datasets containing various types of data and understand how each type serves different analytical purposes.

3-5.B.4.2a.description: Use datasets that include only variables necessary to answer the stated question.

6-8.B.4.2a.description: Work with datasets that include rates and derived variables that combine multiple measurements.

9-10.B.4.2a.description: Work with datasets that include time-series data at different intervals to detect various patterns.

11-12.B.4.2a.description: Create and use expected value models to support data-based decision making.

3-5.B.4.2b.description: Use datasets with both numerical and categorical variables.

6-8.B.4.2b.description: Work with datasets that have multiple variables that can suggest or answer different questions.

9-10.B.4.2b.description: Understand and work with different observation structures beyond individual units.

11-12.B.4.2b.description: Work with multiple datasets that combine multiple types of data and combine and transform the different types.

6-8.B.4.2c.description: Work with datasets that show natural variation and understand why values differ.

9-10.B.4.2c.description: Work with merged datasets that align different time scales and observation structures.

11-12.B.4.2c.description: Work with complex derived variables and understand their calculation methods.

B.4.3.description: Size: Work with datasets of increasing size in both number of observations and variables and arrange data in increasingly complex formats to facilitate meaningful analysis.

3-5.B.4.3a.description: Work with datasets with up to 4 variables and up to 50 observations.

6-8.B.4.3a.description: Work with datasets with up to 20 variables and over 100 observations.

9-10.B.4.3a.description: Work with datasets with over 20 variables and over 1000 observations.

11-12.B.4.3a.description: Work with very large datasets multiple thousands of observations.

3-5.B.4.3b.description: Recognize the difference between numerical and categorical data and choose the appropriate type for a particular measurement.

6-8.B.4.3b.description: Understand how categorical variables can be used to create meaningful subsets.

9-10.B.4.3b.description: Transform data between wide and long formats based on analysis needs.

11-12.B.4.3b.description: Use selection, sampling, and transformation tools to navigate very large datasets.

B.4.4.description: Complexity of structure: Manipulate and combine data in increasingly complex ways to reveal new insights and patterns.

3-5.B.4.4a.description: Combine information from two simple datasets about the same objects or events.

6-8.B.4.4a.description: Work with datasets where the row isn't a single observation but something more complex (e.g., average, nested cases).

9-10.B.4.4a.description: Merge multiple datasets while maintaining appropriate observation structure.

11-12.B.4.4a.description: Design and implement data structures that can accommodate longitudinal data and multiple levels of aggregation.

3-5.B.4.4b.description: Create new variables through simple calculations or combinations of existing data.

6-8.B.4.4b.description: Work with datasets that include derived or transformed variables, including creating categorical variables from numerical data.

9-10.B.4.4b.description: Transform complex variables into more interpretable forms using student-relatable benchmarks.

11-12.B.4.4b.description: Handle data aggregation across different observation structures and time scales.

3-5.B.4.4c.description: Convert data between different basic formats (e.g., from tally marks to numbers).

6-8.B.4.4c.description: Understand how categorical variables can be used to create meaningful subsets.

11-12.B.4.4c.description: Create flexible organizational systems that can handle both structured and unstructured data sources.

11-12.B.4.4d.description: Develop documentation systems for complex data structures that track relationships and dependencies between variables.

C.description: Analysis and Modeling Techniques: This strand focuses on the process of analyzing data. Analyzing data includes many different techniques such as examining single and multi-variable patterns, measures of centrality, variability, and uncertainty. Knowing which techniques to use on which types of data to answer which questions is as important as the skills to conduct analysis techniques. Additionally, understanding simulation and the relational nature of data is important to the analysis process, as is the use of technological tools for analysis and modeling.

C1.description: Summarizing Data: Raw data often is not useful for answering questions, making claims, or telling a story. In order to derive understanding it is usually useful to have a summary of the data which provides measures of the centrality, spread, and shape of the dataset.

C.1.1.description: Measures of center: Analyze large datasets by measuring their central tendency while considering the context and distribution of the data.

3-5.C.1.1a.description: Calculate summaries for categorical and numeric data, focusing on total and typical values.

6-8.C.1.1a.description: Identify measures of center as statistical values that represent the central tendency of data sets.

9-10.C.1.1a.description: Identify appropriate ways to summarize numerical or categorical data using frequency tables, graphical displays, and numerical summary statistics.

11-12.C.1.1a.description: Explore the sensitivity of the mean to outliers compared to the median.

6-8.C.1.1b.description: Explain what measures of center are useful for and their limitations.

11-12.C.1.1b.description: Discuss instances when to use the mean or median based on the context and data distribution (e.g., skewed vs. symmetric distribution).

C.1.2.description: Measures of spread: Examine dataset variability by applying measures of spread to identify and quantify outliers.

3-5.C.1.2a.description: Calculate the range for numerical data.

6-8.C.1.2a.description: Categorically identify the presence of potential outliers in a dataset.

9-10.C.1.2a.description: Calculate standard deviation from mean or interquartile range.

11-12.C.1.2a.description: Numerically operationalize the meaning of an "outlier" using standard deviation as a measure of variability and a modified boxplot.

9-10.C.1.2b.description: Use standard deviation as a measure of variability and a modified boxplot for identifying outliers.

C.1.3.description: Shape: Identify the distribution of data points, including clusters, gaps, symmetry, skewness, and modes. Use these patterns to understand data spread and their impact on measures like the mean and median.

3-5.C.1.3a.description: Describe the number of clusters, symmetric or not, and gaps. e.g., dot plot of test scores might show a cluster at 80-90% meaning most students did well and a gap at 50-60% meaning few students struggled

6-8.C.1.3a.description: Describe whether data is symmetric or asymmetric and the number of modes.

9-10.C.1.3a.description: Acknowledge that in a tie for the mode the distribution is bi-modal.

11-12.C.1.3a.description: Explain how the shape of a distribution influences the relationship between measures of center. e.g., in symmetric distributions - the mean and median are close, in a right-skewed distribution - the mean is greater than the median, in a left-skewed distribution - the mean is less than the median

9-10.C.1.3b.description: Understand how the data is distributed across the range of data. e.g., if the data is skewed to one side of the range

C.1.4.description: Frequency tables: Organize data into frequency tables based on shared characteristics. Summarize data using counts, fractions, relative frequencies, or proportions to enable comparisons and generalizations. Understand the implications of choices made when creating and interpreting frequency tables.

3-5.C.1.4a.description: Summarize data with fractions, relative frequencies, proportions, or percentages to make comparisons.

6-8.C.1.4a.description: Generate a frequency table to summarize raw categorical data.

9-10.C.1.4a.description: Generate a relative frequency table to make comparisons and to generalize results.

11-12.C.1.4a.description: Discuss implications of choices made when generating a frequency table.

C.1.5.description: Missingness: Identify and describe missing data numerically and categorically. Distinguish between missing values and true zeros. Understand how missing data impacts relationships, patterns, and models in data interpretation.

3-5.C.1.5a.description: Categorically describe the absence of data.

9-10.C.1.5a.description: Adjust analyses in light of missing values.

11-12.C.1.5a.description: Describe how missing data affects analysis and resulting relationships, patterns, or models.

6-8.C.1.5b.description: Recognize the difference between the absence of data, and "zero."

C.1.6.description: Metadata: Recognize metadata as information about data, including its source, type, and structure. Use metadata to organize, summarize, and analyze data effectively, supporting interpretation and decision-making.

3-5.C.1.6a.description: Understand the definition and use of metadata (e.g., date and time, text, continuous, geolocation).

6-8.C.1.6a.description: Comprehend, in an informal sense, the value of information contained in metadata (e.g., date and time, text, continuous, geolocation).

9-10.C.1.6a.description: Apply understanding of metadata (e.g., date and time, text, continuous, geolocation) to summarize and analyze data numerically, in tables and through visualizations.

11-12.C.1.6a.description: Reasonably ideate on some potential modeling approaches when given the metadata (e.g., date and time, text, continuous, geolocation) for a dataset.

C2.description: Identifying Patterns and Relationships in Data: A primary use of data is in understanding patterns and relationships across different variables and scenarios. As all data contains variability it is important to understand and analyze distributions both within and across variables.

C.2.1.description: Comparing variables: Identify similarities and differences between variables and explore potential associations. Use distributions, numerical summaries, and simulations to compare groups based on numerical or categorical data.

3-5.C.2.1a.description: Observe whether or not there appears to be an association between two variables. e.g., student height compared to shoe size vs. student height compared to favorite color

6-8.C.2.1a.description: Use reasoning about distributions to compare two groups based on quantitative variables.

9-10.C.2.1a.description: Use numerical measures such as average, standard deviation and quartiles to compare two groups.

11-12.C.2.1a.description: Use simulations to investigate associations between two categorical variables and to compare groups.

C.2.2.description: Understanding distributions: Represent data visually and numerically to describe how outcomes occur and compare groups. Use variability to interpret distribution shape, support statistical reasoning, and assess population estimates.

3-5.C.2.2a.description: Understand that the distribution of a categorical or numerical variable represents how often a specific outcome occurs.

6-8.C.2.2a.description: Represent the variability of numerical variables using appropriate displays (e.g., dotplots, boxplots).

9-10.C.2.2a.description: Quantify variability in distributions using numerical measures.

11-12.C.2.2a.description: Use variability in distributions to engage in statistical reasoning.

3-5.C.2.2b.description: Recognize that distributions can be used to compare two groups.

9-10.C.2.2b.description: Recognize the relationship between variability and the shape of a distribution.

11-12.C.2.2b.description: Understand and interpret variability in sampling distributions and how it impacts population estimates.

C.2.3.description: Defining relationships: Organize, visualize, and analyze data to identify patterns, trends, and associations. Use statistical measures and graphs to interpret relationships and make predictions.

3-5.C.2.3a.description: Create time-series graphs to determine change in variable over time.

6-8.C.2.3a.description: Employ complex graphs (e.g., bar graphs, line graphs) and basic statistical concepts (e.g., mean, median, mode) to describe patterns and identify trends, similarities, and differences within data.

9-10.C.2.3a.description: Describe associations between two categorical variables using measures such as difference in proportions and relative risk.

11-12.C.2.3a.description: Conduct linear regression analysis to find the best-fit.

3-5.C.2.3b.description: Use data collected through surveys or experiments (e.g., heights of fellow classmates) and use spreadsheets to visualize trends and relationships

6-8.C.2.3b.description: Create scatterplots and add line of best fit.

9-10.C.2.3b.description: Analyze data to uncover correlations, trends, and groupings such as clustering that inform decision-making processes across diverse fields.

11-12.C.2.3b.description: Construct prediction intervals and confidence intervals to determine plausible values of a predicted observation or a population characteristic.

3-5.C.2.3c.description: Use no-code or low-code data science tools. e.g., CODAP, Desmos, Google sheets

C.2.4.description: Analyzing non-traditional data: Examine data beyond numbers, including sounds, textures, and text. Categorize sensory inputs, track word frequencies, and analyze data from sensors and IoT devices to identify patterns and trends.

3-5.C.2.4a.description: Identify word frequencies from a simple text (e.g., paragraph or story).

6-8.C.2.4a.description: Compare word frequencies across multiple texts to identify patterns and create simple visualizations from that text data.

9-10.C.2.4a.description: Analyze data from sensors and IoT devices to track trends and monitor changes over time. e.g., smart thermostats and lighting systems for energy monitoring, wearable fitness trackers for health and activity data

11-12.C.2.4a.description: Generate a word cloud of a given text after standardizing (e.g., all lower case), stemming, and removing stop words.

3-5.C.2.4b.description: Collect and analyze simple sensor data (e.g., temperature readings over a day).

6-8.C.2.4b.description: Explore patterns in audio data (e.g., analyzing sound waves for volume and frequency).

9-10.C.2.4b.description: Understand that geographic data can be visualized using maps, and it can be represented as points (e.g., latitude and longitude) and areas (e.g., GeoJSON).

C.2.5.description: Machine learning: Use data to build decision trees, explore classification and clustering, and understand how machine learning optimizes predictions through algorithms like gradient descent.

3-5.C.2.5a.description: Use data from surveys (e.g., favorite snacks) and then have students use this data to build a decision tree.

6-8.C.2.5a.description: Learn to use simple diagrams (e.g., decision trees using small relatable examples) to make important decisions for everyday choices.

9-10.C.2.5a.description: Explore machine learning basics (e.g., classification and clustering) to make predictions with data.

11-12.C.2.5a.description: Explore how gradient descent optimizes loss functions and powers machine learning applications like neural networks.

C3.description: Variability in Data: Variability is omnipresent within data and datasets. Working with data depends on understanding, explaining, and quantifying variability of all forms (variability within a group, between different groups, or between samples).

C.3.1.description: Describing variability: Identify differences within data by sorting, grouping, and organizing characteristics. Use statistical and simulation methods to represent and analyze variability, connecting it to real-world uncertainty and probabilistic processes.

3-5.C.3.1a.description: Sort, order, group, or otherwise organize objects or their representations to answer questions.

6-8.C.3.1a.description: Identify probabilistic processes that simulate various forms of categorical variability, including uniform and normal distributions. e.g., spinner, dice, random draw

9-10.C.3.1a.description: Describe methods (e.g., statistical, simulation) to analyze variability in data and connect it to known or hypothesized processes in a specific domain.

11-12.C.3.1a.description: Apply statistical or simulation methods to model variability to explore uncertainty in real-world situations.

3-5.C.3.1b.description: Categorically describe the center, spread, and shape of a simple distribution and understand what each of these descriptions refer to.

6-8.C.3.1b.description: Illustrate variability in a dataset by determining how key descriptive features are represented.

6-8.C.3.1c.description: Evaluate how visualizations, models, or predictions account for variation at an appropriate level.

C.3.2.description: Comparing variability: Examine differences between groups by analyzing measures of spread, such as range and standard deviation. Utilize visualizations like box plots and apply statistical methods, including mean, median, and standard deviation, to compare datasets, assess variability, and uncover patterns in data distributions and models.

3-5.C.3.2a.description: Understand how data varies by exploring spread (e.g., range) and comparing qualities (e.g., brightness or temperature).

6-8.C.3.2a.description: Use visualizations (e.g., box plots) to compare variability across datasets.

9-10.C.3.2a.description: Use simple statistics including mean, median, range, standard deviation, etc. to compare data distributions.

11-12.C.3.2a.description: Explore variability through statistical methods, such as analyzing residuals or variance in linear models.

C.3.3.description: Understanding sources of variability: Recognize measurement errors and natural variability in data. Assess data quality, identify outliers, and refine models using statistical and contextual analysis.

3-5.C.3.3a.description: Identify and explain simple measurement error. e.g., different students' get varying results when measuring the same object

6-8.C.3.3a.description: Consider both context and the characteristics of a dataset to determine whether a given data point is reasonable. e.g., meaningful outliner, erroneous outlier

9-10.C.3.3a.description: Consider variability as a key component of informal inference by questioning whether observed differences are meaningful or not. e.g., phone battery lasts 6 hours one day and 4 the next—is this a real difference in battery life, or just normal variation from daily use

11-12.C.3.3a.description: Estimate and describe errors between predictions and actual outcomes. e.g., residuals, misclassification rates

3-5.C.3.3b.description: Identify potential sources of natural variability in a given measure based on knowledge of the data context. e.g., plants can be different heights, plants grow taller over time, plants grow differently in different areas in the garden

6-8.C.3.3b.description: Relate sources of variability to domain-specific phenomena as described in the relevant domain standards. e.g., Next Gen Science Standards, Mathematics Common Core State Standards, C3 Framework

9-10.C.3.3b.description: Identify categorical options for measuring "best" fit from data points to provided estimates. e.g., line or curve for a scatterplot, mean for a distribution

11-12.C.3.3b.description: Analyze error patterns to assess model performance. e.g., residual plot, confusion matrix

9-10.C.3.3c.description: Consider both context and the characteristics/source of a dataset to determine how "messy" a dataset may be due to measurement error. e.g., faulty sensors, inaccurate or inappropriate measurements

11-12.C.3.3c.description: Use insights from error analysis to improve the model. e.g., in linear regression, add a variable or use a curve; in classification, balance the groups or adjust the cutoff

9-10.C.3.3d.description: Use errors to improve the AI and/or machine learning model.

C.3.4.description: Variability in our computational world: Explore how AI model outputs vary based on training data, labeling, and bias. Understand how generative AI and pre-trained models use large datasets to make inferences and how variability in data impacts outcomes.

6-8.C.3.4a.description: Conceptualize how the output of AI models such as LLMs vary along a variety of dimensions.

9-10.C.3.4a.description: Acknowledge how variability in the training data for generative AI influences bias in its output. e.g., facial recognition, ownership of DNA data

11-12.C.3.4a.description: Appreciate that many AI tools are pre-trained with large quantities of data so that inferences can be drawn on smaller sample sizes.

6-8.C.3.4b.description: Determine how labeling happens and how it affects the variability of the output of models. e.g., training set that labels dogs vs. cats, consider connections to bias

C4.description: Digital Tools of Data Analysis: While some datasets can be explored by hand, as they get bigger and more complex it becomes necessary to use digital tools for analysing data. It is important to understand which tools to use for which application or scenario, the affordances and tradeoffs, and the ethical considerations of using certain tools.

C.4.1.description: Tool application: Use digital tools to summarize data and create visualizations. Apply these tools to identify patterns, clean and prepare data, perform analysis, and build models for simulations to explore relationships and trends.

3-5.C.4.1a.description: Summarize data that is represented in a digital tool.

6-8.C.4.1a.description: Summarize data across multiple categories using a digital tool.

9-10.C.4.1a.description: Identify relationships and patterns using a digital tool.

11-12.C.4.1a.description: Create models to perform simulations using a digital tool.

6-8.C.4.1b.description: Create single variable visualizations using a digital tool.

9-10.C.4.1b.description: Clean and wrangle data using a digital tool.

11-12.C.4.1b.description: Perform data analysis using a digital tool.

6-8.C.4.1c.description: Identify relationships and patterns using a digital tool.

9-10.C.4.1c.description: Create multi-variable visualizations using digital tools.

C.4.2.description: Tool ethics: Examine how digital tools influence access, privacy, and bias, shaping opportunities and challenges in technology use. Consider the broader ethical and societal impacts of AI, including its role in decision-making, accountability, and policy.

6-8.C.4.2a.description: Describe how digital tools can be used to provide equitable access to learning experiences.

9-10.C.4.2a.description: Describe the ethical limitations (e.g., environmental, privacy, copyright, hallucination) of using AI tools.

11-12.C.4.2a.description: Critique the societal effect of AI by exploring issues surrounding bias, accountability, and transparency in decision-making using AI tools, as well as the effects on privacy, jobs, and policy.

C.4.3.description: Tool evaluation: Assess the technical limitations of digital tools and compare no-code, low-code, and high-code solutions based on their capabilities and use cases.

9-10.C.4.3a.description: Identify the technical limitations of a digital tool.

11-12.C.4.3a.description: Identify differences between a no-code, low-code, or high-code digital tool.

C.4.4.description: Tool selection: Choose the appropriate no-code, low-code, or high-code digital tool based on the task. Use multiple tools throughout the data investigation process and explore how digital tools are applied in the workforce.

3-5.C.4.4a.description: Select a no-code digital tool that is suited for the intended task.

6-8.C.4.4a.description: Select a no-code or low-code digital tool that is suited for the intended task.

9-10.C.4.4a.description: Select a no-code, low-code or high-code digital tool that is suited for the intended task.

11-12.C.4.4a.description: Select multiple digital tools suited for different tasks throughout the data investigation process.

11-12.C.4.4b.description: Describe how digital tools are used in the workforce.

C.4.5.description: The role of code in data analysis: Explore how block coding and computer code automate and enhance data analysis. Understand how coding enables reproducible processes and compare its advantages and limitations to no-code and low-code tools.

6-8.C.4.5a.description: Explore the basics of block coding in data investigation processes.

9-10.C.4.5a.description: Recognize how computer code can automate data investigation processes.

11-12.C.4.5a.description: Recognize how computer code can be used to produce reproducible data analysis processes.

6-8.C.4.5b.description: Explore the basics of block coding in data analysis processes.

9-10.C.4.5b.description: Recognize how computer code can automate data analysis processes.

11-12.C.4.5b.description: Recognize the advantages and limitations of using computer code compared to no-code or low-code tools.

C.4.6.description: Tool accessibility for diverse learners: Understand how digital tools can support a broad range of diverse learners. Evaluate their effectiveness and impact, and explore inclusive data representations.

3-5.C.4.6a.description: Identify tools that make data more accessible, such as screen-readers, captions, or tactile graphs.

6-8.C.4.6a.description: Explore why it’s important to present data in multiple formats to ensure all learners can understand it.

9-10.C.4.6a.description: Explore how to communicate with data while prioritizing accessibility.

11-12.C.4.6a.description: Design data visualizations that include accessible features such alt-text and text descriptions.

6-8.C.4.6b.description: Explore how digital tools support diverse learners to analyze data. e.g., immersive readers, speech-to-text, translators, sonification

9-10.C.4.6b.description: Critique the levels of accessibility of digital tools and representations of data.

11-12.C.4.6b.description: Examine how policies, limitations, and technological advancements impact the development of accessible digital tools.

6-8.C.4.6c.description: Discuss how the lack of accessible digital tools can exclude people from participating in data analysis.

C5.description: Models of Data: Interpreting, creating, and using models is a central component of working with data. Models are both a way to analyze data and a source of data.

C.5.1.description: Understanding modeling: Analyze patterns and relationships in data using graphs, tables, and models. Explore tools like decision trees and neural networks, assess assumptions, and distinguish correlation from causation in real-world contexts.

3-5.C.5.1a.description: Understand that grouping objects by shared characteristics creates rules that can be used to classify and categorize new objects.

6-8.C.5.1a.description: Explore how relationships in data connect characteristics, including patterns like increasing, decreasing, or no connection.

9-10.C.5.1a.description: Recognize that bivariate relationships between numerical features can be examined using both linear and non-linear associations.

11-12.C.5.1a.description: Discern that different models, such as decision trees and neural networks, analyze patterns and relationships in data to make predictions.

3-5.C.5.1b.description: Recognize that patterns and relationships in data provide different kinds of information.

6-8.C.5.1b.description: Recognize that models simplify complex systems and have limitations.

9-10.C.5.1b.description: Investigate real-world examples where correlation does not imply causation.

11-12.C.5.1b.description: Assess relationships in the context of uncertainty, bias, and reliability of the data.

3-5.C.5.1c.description: Discuss how data relationships help describe real-world phenomena. e.g., taller plants tend to be older

6-8.C.5.1c.description: Recognize that relationships in data do not always imply causation. e.g., ice cream sales and shark attacks both increase in the summer, but one doesn't cause the other

11-12.C.5.1c.description: Investigate how assumptions and bias influence a model's results.

C.5.2.description: Creating models: Develop an understanding of patterns and relationships. Use data and technology to build and refine models. Advance these skills by constructing complex models that incorporate multiple variables, assess assumptions, and improve predictions.

3-5.C.5.2a.description: Predict whether an object belongs to a group or category based on its characteristics.

6-8.C.5.2a.description: Identify relationships between variables and represent them using tables, graphs, or diagrams (e.g., decision trees, flowcharts).

9-10.C.5.2a.description: Construct and analyze models to represent linear and non-linear relationships in data.

11-12.C.5.2a.description: Develop models that incorporate multiple variables and explicitly consider interactions between them.

3-5.C.5.2b.description: Distinguish patterns from relationships in data.

6-8.C.5.2b.description: Use simple mathematical or computational models (e.g., statistical summaries, spreadsheet formulas) to describe patterns and relationships in data.

9-10.C.5.2b.description: Use technology to create, test, and refine models.

11-12.C.5.2b.description: Use computational methods, coding, or machine learning techniques to build and refine models.

6-8.C.5.2c.description: Test and refine models by comparing predictions to actual data values.

9-10.C.5.2c.description: Evaluate and improve models by comparing predictions to observed data.

11-12.C.5.2c.description: Assess assumptions, limitations, and biases in models to evaluate their impact on predictions in real-world scenarios.

D.description: Interpreting Problems and Results: This strand focuses on justification and explanation of reasoning when making inferences, claims, or suggestions from data within the context and processes of the dataset collection and analysis. An important component of interpreting results is understanding the relationship between questions, problems and datasets. Formulating a strong question or identifying a problem that can be addressed with data affects the opportunities for interpretation and results from the data. Additionally, the applicability of inferences and claims that are made are constrained by the sample, population, and context of the data.

D1.description: Making and Justifying Claims: As all data contains variability, it is important to use probabilistic thinking and language when making claims from data. This requires paying attention not only to patterns and comparisons within and across variables but also such things as expected and prior values, sample sizes, and significance.

D.1.1.description: Probabilistic language: When communicating with others, employ both plain-language and clear vocabulary to regularly describe degrees of uncertainty, both formally and informally as a thinking habit.

3-5.D.1.1a.description: Formulate a guess or hypothesis and identify informal vocabulary to convey your level of confidence. e.g., I strongly believe most of my classmates ride the bus to school because XX or YY

6-8.D.1.1a.description: Express a finding and quantify your confidence in it by stating the degree of certainty regarding the result. e.g., I am highly confident that a majority of students in my area ride the bus to school, based on separate sources' estimations of 60%, 62.3%, and 65% of students ride the bus to school

9-10.D.1.1a.description: Clearly state a result or finding and indicate the level of certainty regarding a formal statistical concept alongside an informal evaluation of the likelihood of the event.

11-12.D.1.1a.description: Clearly state the result or finding and indicate the level of certainty regarding the statistical analysis and the quality of the evidence (e.g., dataset or source characteristics, similar findings in alternative data) as justification.

Adv.D.1.1a.description: Clearly state a result or finding, along with the degree of certainty, using two or more advanced statistical methods (e.g., probability distributions, t-tests, z-tests, or bootstrapping/simulation), while justifying the conclusions with evidence (e.g., dataset or source characteristics, similar findings in alternative data) quality indicators like dataset characteristics, source reliability, and corroborating findings from alternative data.

D.1.2.description: Priors and updates: When encountering new data, integrate probabilistic thinking into everyday situations by explicating prior assumptions and the impact of new data / evidence on those assumptions.

3-5.D.1.2a.description: Record a guess about the world, compare the initial assumption to new findings from data, and assess the extent to which the original assumption should change in light of new evidence.

6-8.D.1.2a.description: Recognize that an assumption should change somewhat, but may not need to change entirely, based on the "strength of" or degree of confidence in new evidence.

9-10.D.1.2a.description: Analyze how confirmation bias and availability bias influence the way individuals evaluate new information, especially regarding their existing beliefs and assumptions.

11-12.D.1.2a.description: Summarize previous assumptions and potential updates in written conclusions from a data analysis, and identify any known contradictory findings to mitigate confirmation bias.

Adv.D.1.2a.description: Explain Bayes Theorem in formal conditional probability statements: P(A|B) = (P(A) * P(B|A)) / P(B), where A is the event in question and B is the event of new evidence related to A.

6-8.D.1.2b.description: Connect previous assumptions about a problem to the level of certainty in a finding by using the terms “prior assumption,” “new data/evidence," and “my updated assumption.”

9-10.D.1.2b.description: Relate assumptions about a problem to the certainty of findings based on new evidence.

11-12.D.1.2b.description: Describe Bayes Theorem by explaining how it relates to conditional probability, which includes the probability of an event occurring, the probability of that event given the evidence is true, and the probability that the evidence itself is true.

Adv.D.1.2b.description: Apply Bayes Theorem to an example result in an academic research finding or discussion.

11-12.D.1.2c.description: Apply the logic of Bayes Theorem to determine whether a data-based claim in the media was accurately explained.

D.1.3.description: Expected value: When making a decision about uncertain outcomes in the future, integrate probabilistic thinking into everyday decisions by applying expected value (magnitude x probability) to appropriate situations.

3-5.D.1.3a.description: Discuss the relationship between magnitude and probability. e.g., is a small chance of a large-sized event equivalent to a medium chance of a medium-sized event

6-8.D.1.3a.description: Numerically compare the impact of two events with different magnitudes and probabilities to determine which scenario is preferable. e.g., financial problem; 10% chance of receiving $100 vs. 50% chance of receiving $50

9-10.D.1.3a.description: Identify and accurately employ the Expected Value equation (EV = P (Xi) * Xi) across multiple contexts to compare scenarios involving multiple trials. e.g., insurance policies, lotteries

11-12.D.1.3a.description: Justify the Expected Value equation (EV = P (Xi) * Xi) with formal probability statements and by explaining the Law of Large numbers.

9-10.D.1.3b.description: Solve a real-world comparison problem using a digital spreadsheet, such as selecting insurance policies or entering different lotteries. e.g., choosing insurance policies, entering different lotteries

11-12.D.1.3b.description: Apply the Expected Value equation to assess its fitness for the problem by determining the accuracy of the estimate based on the number of trials conducted. e.g., flipping a coin 100 times and determining if getting heads 30 times is reasonable when the expected value is getting heads 50 times

D.1.4.description: Explaining significance: Clearly describe the basic logic of statistical significance to others, differentiating between significance, the size of an effect, and the statistical power of an analysis. Recognize what statistical significance can reveal and cannot reveal about a phenomenon.

3-5.D.1.4a.description: Describe how "unusual" a result may be compared to an otherwise expected outcome in a given situation. e.g., flipping a coin 10 times and getting 10 heads is highly unlikely

6-8.D.1.4a.description: Recognize and describe random chance in a given situation, and explain whether a result is unusual by comparing it to what is expected from random chance. e.g., flipping a coin 10 times and getting 8 heads is less common than 5 heads and 5 tails, but still possible due to random chance

9-10.D.1.4a.description: Identify situations when distinguishing from random chance is especially important. e.g., medical drug trial, public policy implementation

11-12.D.1.4a.description: Explain the concept of statistical significance (e.g., including its role in distinguishing meaningful results from random chance) in plain language and the limitations of significance testing (e.g., inability to address study design flaws, confounding variables, or real-world validity beyond a narrow model comparison).

Adv.D.1.4a.description: Identify examples of p-value misuse in the media or academic research.

6-8.D.1.4b.description: Recognize that a unique result may be considered significant if it is substantially different from outcomes in similar situations.

9-10.D.1.4b.description: Describe probability distributions and give real-world examples of how they can represent different types of random events.

11-12.D.1.4b.description: Describe how statistical significance tests are constructed, calculated, and interpreted in the context of chosen probability models and/or assumptions.

Adv.D.1.4b.description: Describe a p-value to without using the language of the "null hypothesis" or "alternative hypothesis."

6-8.D.1.4c.description: Recognize that a unique result may be considered significant if it falls far from the typical range of outcomes in a visualized distribution of results.

9-10.D.1.4c.description: Identify and describe a normal distribution as a possible model for random chance that can be used to determine whether a result is statistically significant.

11-12.D.1.4c.description: Identify real-world instances where assessing statistical significance is crucial (e.g., scientific studies to distinguish actual effects from random variation) while also evaluating the significance claims made by others and recognizing situations where statistical significance is necessary but not sufficient for proving a point.

11-12.D.1.4d.description: Differentiate statistical significance, effect size, and statistical power in simple terms with real-world examples, explaining how each addresses distinct questions in research. e.g., whether outcomes could be connected to random chance, the meaningfulness of impacts in context, the suitability of the analysis approach to the specific data and problems

D.1.5.description: Sampling and simulation: Comfortably identify the purpose of sampling and simulation for making arguments about data, and employ techniques using software to differentiate a real-data result from random chance or “happenstance.”

3-5.D.1.5a.description: Recognize that a sample of a group may or may not reflect the entire group. e.g., if the class's favorite drink for lunch is chocolate milk, does that mean the school's favorite drink for lunch is chocolate milk?

6-8.D.1.5a.description: Evaluate how different sampling methods impact the accurate representation of a population and their ability to generalize findings to other groups.

9-10.D.1.5a.description: Use simulations in a digital software to help determine whether the results of an experiment are likely due to something other than random chance.

11-12.D.1.5a.description: Use simulation-based inferential methods at large N to draw conclusions from a dataset using digital software.

Adv.D.1.5a.description: Execute and correctly interpret the margin of error, confidence interval, and standard deviation in a data analysis software for a given summary statistic.

3-5.D.1.5b.description: Relate the effect of repeated samples to the representativeness of an entire group. e.g., pulling 10 jellybeans from a jar 5 times gives a better estimate of the color distribution than just one handful

6-8.D.1.5b.description: Assess how sample size impacts the accuracy of estimates representing population characteristics.

9-10.D.1.5b.description: Analyze how dataset bias impacts sample results over time by introducing intentional bias sources in digital simulations and observing their effects.

11-12.D.1.5b.description: Identify why simulation can be used to infer conclusions about a population referencing the Law of Large Numbers.

Adv.D.1.5b.description: Describe the relationship between the margin of error, confidence intervals, and standard deviation, in both words and in their formal mathematical definitions.

6-8.D.1.5c.description: Identify the sources of potential bias in a sample or population, and describe how bias may impact the results of an investigation.

9-10.D.1.5c.description: Answer probabilistic questions resulting from a simulation.

11-12.D.1.5c.description: Interpret margin of error and confidence intervals for a given sample.

6-8.D.1.5d.description: Describe what it means for an event to be likely or unlikely using probability. e.g., probability of 0 is unlikely, 1 is very likely, 1:2 is neither likely or unlikely

D.1.6.description: Correlation versus causation: Comfortably separate correlation from causation in a wide variety of situations, building a “first-reaction” thinking habit over time.

3-5.D.1.6a.description: Using graphical displays, informally assess whether or not there is an association between two phenomenon in a data visualization and discuss whether one observation or trend may affect the other.

6-8.D.1.6a.description: Assess simple data to identify potential associations between two variables while considering that correlations do not imply causation and may arise from unobserved factors.

9-10.D.1.6a.description: Recognize that a randomized experiment is the best way to establish evidence for causation and justify a claim through isolating the effect of only one independent variable on another variable at a time.

11-12.D.1.6a.description: Independently identify examples of two dependent variables that are both influenced by a third variable in real-world data. e.g., coffee consumption and lower risk of disease are both affected by an active lifestyle

Adv.D.1.6a.description: Justify a causal relationship in a multivariable dataset with real-world data, including additional datasets gathered from outside sources and connect the analysis to existing research literature.

6-8.D.1.6b.description: Using graphical displays, identify and categorize the type of potential relationship between pairs of numerical variables with terms such as independent, dependent, and covariate.

9-10.D.1.6b.description: Identify spurious correlations in the media and explore other potential causes that may explain these associations when applicable.

11-12.D.1.6b.description: Identify spurious correlations in the media and analyze how they relate to media claims and AI recommendations. e.g., ice cream sales and shark attacks both increase in the summer; they're both linked to hot weather, not each other

Adv.D.1.6b.description: Explain why a chosen analysis method effectively isolates an effect.

D.1.7.description: Randomization: When identifying a potential cause of a phenomenon, clearly describe the usefulness of randomization for constructing an argument with data.

3-5.D.1.7a.description: Recognize that randomization ensures fairness in selection processes and consider the potential consequences of non-blind selection methods. e.g., picking a raffle champion, prizes from a jar, candy of different sizes from a treat bag without looking
